messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Network Engineer
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 44

She sits in the chair across from me with the careful posture of someone used to managing crises—back straight, hands still, eyes scanning the room before they settle. She is a network engineer for a regional telecom company, a job that demands she anticipate failures, reroute traffic, keep systems running even when circuits overload. She tells me she is good at this, at staying calm when something breaks. But there is one thing she cannot reroute.

The story starts two years ago, in the summer. Her daughter, then four years old, began to bruise easily, to wake up with fevers that came and went. A general practitioner sent them to the children’s hospital. Within seventy-two hours they had a name for it: acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She remembers the word “acute” hitting her chest before the rest of it registered. She remembers how the air in the consultation room seemed to thin, how the doctor’s mouth kept moving but the sounds were underwater. She remembers her ex-husband—already distant, already halfway out the door—saying, “We’ll get through this,” as if he were reading a script.

The treatment protocol stretched across months: chemotherapy, spinal taps, isolation days when a common cold could mean an ICU stay. She took a leave of absence from work initially, but the bills piled up, and her divorce was finalized during week six of her daughter’s first round of treatment. She went back to her job part-time, then full-time, scheduling her daughter’s appointments around system upgrades and overnight maintenance windows. She learned to compartmentalize. At the hospital she was the mother who never cried in front of the nurses. At work she was the engineer who could trace a packet drop across three time zones.

But the trauma does not stay compartmentalized.

Now, her daughter is in maintenance phase. The doctors say the prognosis is excellent. She should feel relief. Instead, she feels like she is holding her breath underwater, waiting for the next surge. She does not sleep through the night. If her daughter coughs in the next room, she is up, pulse thudding in her temples, already halfway to the bedroom before she realizes it is only a cough. She has become attuned to the sound of her daughter’s breathing—she can tell from the rhythm alone if it is obstructed, if it is too shallow. When it is quiet she finds herself listening for it, which means it is never really quiet.

At work, she has started to avoid certain tasks. She used to run the quarterly disaster-recovery simulation; now she volunteers to update documentation instead. When the fire alarm goes off during a routine drill, her hands shake for the rest of the shift, and she walks out to the parking lot three times to check her phone, even though she knows her daughter is at school. She has told no one about this. She deletes the call history to the pediatric oncology hotline even though she does not call it anymore.

The divorce, she says, was not about the illness. It was already unraveling. But she wonders now if she pushed him away on purpose, because she could not bear to have one more person she might lose. She lives alone with her daughter in a small apartment near the hospital. She has not dated. She has not gone to a single playdate or birthday party for other children since the diagnosis. She tells herself she is just busy. But the truth is she cannot sit in a room full of healthy children without feeling a kind of dread she cannot name, a sense that the next routine symptom will be the one that changes everything.

When I ask her what she thinks about most, she says: “The first night in the hospital. The beeping. The way the IV pump sounded when it was about to alarm. I can still hear it.” She hears it sometimes when she tries to fall asleep, so she stays up late configuring network switches, running diagnostic scripts, anything to drown out the sound. She is tired. But staying busy is the only way she knows to keep the story from replaying—the story she has told herself a hundred times, always waiting for a different ending that never comes.
